vsm1.1:85.1:
85. (d) As regards the next kind called virtue concerning requisites: here is the text: “Reflecting wisely,
he uses the robe only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies,
flies, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of concealing the private parts. Reflecting wisely,
he uses alms food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance
and continuance of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the life of purity: ‘Thus I shall put
a stop to old feelings and shall not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.’
Reflecting wisely, he uses the resting place only for the purpose of protection from cold, for protection from heat,
for protection from contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of warding
off the perils of climate and enjoying retreat. Reflecting wisely, he uses the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick
only for protection from arisen hurtful feelings and for complete immunity from affliction” (M I 10). Herein,
reflecting wisely is reflecting as the means and as the way; by knowing, by reviewing, is the meaning.
vsm1.1:85.2:
And here it is the reviewing stated in the way beginning, “For protection from cold”
that should be understood as “reflecting wisely.”
vsm1.1:86.1: 86. Herein, the robe is any one of those beginning with the inner cloth.
vsm1.1:86.2: He uses: he employs; dresses in as inner cloth, or puts on as upper garment.
vsm1.1:86.3: Only is a phrase signifying invariability in the definition of a limit of a purpose;
vsm1.1:86.4: the purpose in the meditator’s making use of the robes is that much only, namely, protection from cold, etc., not more than that.
vsm1.1:86.5:
From cold: from any kind of cold arisen either through disturbance of elements
internally or through change in temperature externally.
vsm1.1:86.6: For protection: for the purpose of warding off;
vsm1.1:86.7: for the purpose of eliminating it so that it may not arouse affliction in the body.
vsm1.1:86.8: For when the body is afflicted by cold, the distracted mind cannot be wisely exerted.
vsm1.1:86.9: That is why the Blessed One permitted the robe to be used for protection from cold.
vsm1.1:86.11: except that from heat means from the heat of fire, the origin of which should be understood as forest fires, and so on.
vsm1.1:87.1: 87. From contact with gadflies and flies, wind and burning and creeping things: here gadflies are flies that bite;
vsm1.1:87.4: Wind is distinguished as that with dust and that without dust.
vsm1.1:87.5: Burning is burning of the sun.
vsm1.1:87.6:
Creeping things are any long creatures such as snakes and so on that move by crawling.
Contact with them is of two kinds: contact by being bitten and contact by being touched.
vsm1.1:87.7: And that does not worry him who sits with a robe on. So he uses it for the purpose of protection from such things.
vsm1.1:88.1: 88. Only: the word is repeated in order to define a subdivision of the invariable purpose;
vsm1.1:88.2: for the concealment of the private parts is an invariable purpose; the others are purposes periodically.
vsm1.1:88.3: Herein, private parts are any parts of the pudendum.
vsm1.1:88.4: For when a member is disclosed, conscience (hiri) is disturbed (kuppati), offended.
vsm1.1:88.5: It is called “private parts” (hirikopīna) because of the disturbance of conscience (hiri-kopana).
vsm1.1:88.6: For the purpose of concealing the private parts: for the purpose of the concealment of those private parts.
vsm1.1:88.7: As well as the reading “hiriko-pīna-paṭicchādanatthaṃ there is a reading “hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ.”
vsm1.1:89.1: 89. Alms food is any sort of food.
vsm1.1:89.2:
For any sort of nutriment is called “alms food” (piṇḍapāta—lit. “lump-dropping”) because of its having
been dropped (patitattā) into a bhikkhu’s bowl during his alms round (piṇḍolya).
vsm1.1:89.3: Or alms food (piṇḍapāta) is the dropping (pāta) of the lumps (piṇḍa);
vsm1.1:89.4: it is the concurrence (sannipāta), the collection, of alms (bhikkhā) obtained here and there, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:89.5: Neither for amusement: neither for the purpose of amusement, as with village boys, etc.; for the sake of sport, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:89.6: Nor for intoxication: not for the purpose of intoxication, as with boxers, etc.;
vsm1.1:89.7: for the sake of intoxication with strength and for the sake of intoxication with manhood, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:89.8: Nor for smartening: not for the purpose of smartening, as with royal concubines, courtesans, etc.;
vsm1.1:89.9: for the sake of plumpness in all the limbs, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:89.10: Nor for embellishment: not for the purpose of embellishment, as with actors, dancers, etc.;
vsm1.1:89.11: for the sake of a clear skin and complexion, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:90.1: 90. And here the clause neither for amusement is stated for the purpose of abandoning support for delusion;
vsm1.1:90.2: nor for intoxication is said for the purpose of abandoning support for hate;
vsm1.1:90.3: nor for smartening nor for embellishment is said for the purpose of abandoning support for greed.
vsm1.1:90.4: And neither for amusement nor for intoxication is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters for oneself.
vsm1.1:90.5: Nor for smartening nor for embellishment is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters for another.
vsm1.1:90.6:
And the abandoning of both unwise practice and devotion to indulgence of sense
pleasures should be understood as stated by these four.
vsm1.1:90.7: Only has the meaning already stated.
vsm1.1:91.1: 91. Of this body: of this material body consisting of the four great primaries.
vsm1.1:91.2: For the endurance: for the purpose of continued endurance.
vsm1.1:91.3: And continuance: for the purpose of not interrupting life’s continued occurrence,
vsm1.1:91.4: or for the purpose of endurance for a long time.
vsm1.1:91.5:
He makes use of the alms food for the purpose of the endurance, for the purpose of the continuance, of the body,
as the owner of an old house uses props for his house, and as a carter uses axle grease,
not for the purpose of amusement, intoxication, smartening, and embellishment.
vsm1.1:91.6: Furthermore, endurance is a term for the life faculty.
vsm1.1:91.7:
So what has been said as far as the words for the endurance and continuance of this body can
be understood to mean: for the purpose of maintaining the occurrence of the life faculty in this body.
vsm1.1:92.1: 92. For the ending of discomfort: hunger is called “discomfort” in the sense of afflicting.
vsm1.1:92.2: He makes use of alms food for the purpose of ending that, like anointing a wound, like counteracting heat with cold, and so on.
vsm1.1:92.3:
For assisting the life of purity: for the purpose of assisting the life of purity
consisting in the whole dispensation and the life of purity consisting in the path.
vsm1.1:92.4:
For while this bhikkhu is engaged in crossing the desert of existence by means of devotion to the three trainings
depending on bodily strength whose necessary condition is the use of alms food, he makes use of it to assist the life of purity
vsm1.1:92.5: just as those seeking to cross the desert used their child’s flesh,
vsm1.1:92.6: just as those seeking to cross a river use a raft, and just as those seeking to cross the ocean use a ship.
vsm1.1:93.1:
93. Thus I shall put a stop to old feelings and shall not arouse new feelings: thus as a sick man uses medicine,
he uses alms food, thinking: “By use of this alms food I shall put a stop to the old feeling of hunger,
vsm1.1:93.2:
and I shall not arouse a new feeling by immoderate eating, like one of the proverbial brahmans,
that is, one who eats till he has to be helped up by hand, or till his clothes will not meet, or till he rolls
there on the ground, or till crows can peck from his mouth, or until he vomits what he has eaten.
vsm1.1:93.3:
Or alternatively, there is that which is called ‘old feelings’ because, being conditioned by former
kamma, it arises now in dependence on unsuitable immoderate eating
vsm1.1:93.4: —I shall put a stop to that old feeling, forestalling its condition by suitable moderate eating.
vsm1.1:93.5:
And there is that which is called ‘new feeling’ because it will arise in the future in dependence on the accumulation of kamma
consisting in making improper use of the requisite of alms food now
vsm1.1:93.6:
—I shall also not arouse that new feeling, avoiding by means of proper use the production of its root.”
This is how the meaning should be understood here.
vsm1.1:93.7:
What has been shown so far can be understood to include proper use of requisites,
abandoning of devotion to self-mortification, and not giving up lawful bliss (pleasure).
vsm1.1:94.1:
94. And I shall be healthy: “In this body, which exists in dependence on requisites, I shall, by moderate eating,
have health called ‘long endurance’ since there will be no danger of severing the life faculty or interrupting
the continuity of the postures.” Reflecting in this way, he makes use of the alms food
vsm1.1:94.2: as a sufferer from a chronic disease does of his medicine.
vsm1.1:94.3:
And blameless and live in comfort (lit. “and have blamelessness and a comfortable abiding”): he makes use of them
thinking: “I shall have blamelessness by avoiding improper search, acceptance and eating,
vsm1.1:94.4: and I shall have a comfortable abiding by moderate eating.”
vsm1.1:94.5:
Or he does so thinking: “I shall have blamelessness due to absence of such faults as boredom, sloth,
sleepiness, blame by the wise, etc., that have unseemly immoderate eating as their condition;
vsm1.1:94.6: and I shall have a comfortable abiding by producing bodily strength that has seemly moderate eating as its condition.”
vsm1.1:94.7:
Or he does so thinking: “I shall have blamelessness by abandoning the pleasure of lying down,
lolling and torpor, through refraining from eating as much as possible to stuff the belly;
vsm1.1:94.8:
and I shall have a comfortable abiding by controlling the four postures through
eating four or five mouthfuls less than the maximum.”
vsm1.1:94.9:
For this is said: “With four or five lumps still to eat Let him then end by drinking water; For energetic
bhikkhus’ needs This should suffice to live in comfort” (Th 983).
vsm1.1:94.10: Now, what has been shown at this point can be understood as discernment of purpose and practice of the middle way.
vsm1.1:95.1: 95. Resting place (senāsana): this is the bed (sena) and seat (āsana).
vsm1.1:95.2: For wherever one sleeps (seti), whether in a monastery or in a lean-to, etc., that is the bed (sena);
vsm1.1:95.3: wherever one seats oneself (āsati), sits (nisīdati), that is the seat (āsana).
vsm1.1:95.5:
For the purpose of warding off the perils of climate and enjoying retreat: the climate
itself in the sense of imperilling (parisahana) is “perils of climate” (utu-parissaya).
vsm1.1:95.6:
Unsuitable climatic conditions that cause mental distraction due to bodily affliction
can be warded off by making use of the resting place;
vsm1.1:95.7: it is for the purpose of warding off these and for the purpose of the pleasure of solitude, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:95.8: Of course, the warding off of the perils of climate is stated by the phrase “protection from cold,” etc., too;
vsm1.1:95.9:
but, just as in the case of making use of the robes the concealment of the private parts
is stated as an invariable purpose while the others are periodical purposes,
vsm1.1:95.10: so here also this last should be understood as mentioned with reference to the invariable warding off of the perils of climate.
vsm1.1:95.11: Or alternatively, this “climate” of the kind stated is just climate;
vsm1.1:95.12: but “perils” are of two kinds: evident perils and concealed perils (see Nidd I 12).
vsm1.1:95.13: Herein, evident perils are lions, tigers, etc.,
vsm1.1:95.14: while concealed perils are greed, hate, and so on.
vsm1.1:95.15:
When a bhikkhu knows and reflects thus in making use of the kind of resting place where these perils do
not, owing to unguarded doors and sight of unsuitable visible objects, etc., cause affliction,
vsm1.1:95.16:
he can be understood as one who “reflecting wisely makes use of the resting
place for the purpose of warding off the perils of climate.”
vsm1.1:96.1:
96. The requisite of medicine as cure for the sick: here “cure” (paccaya = going
against) is in the sense of going against (pati-ayana) illness;
vsm1.1:96.2: in the sense of countering, is the meaning.
vsm1.1:96.3: This is a term for any suitable remedy.
vsm1.1:96.4: It is the medical man’s work (bhisakkassa kammaṃ) because it is permitted by him, thus it is medicine (bhesajja).
vsm1.1:96.5: Or the cure for the sick itself as medicine is “medicine as cure for the sick.”
vsm1.1:96.6: Any work of a medical man such as oil, honey, ghee, etc., that is suitable for one who is sick, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:96.7:
A “requisite” (parikkhāra), however, in such passages as “It is well
supplied with the requisites of a city” (A IV 106) is equipment;
vsm1.1:96.8: in such passages as “The chariot has the requisite of virtue, the axle of jhāna, the wheel of energy” (S V 6) it is an ornament;
vsm1.1:96.9:
in such passages as “The requisites for the life of one who has gone into homelessness
that should be available” (M I 104), it is an accessory.
vsm1.1:96.10: But here both equipment and accessory are applicable.
vsm1.1:96.11: For that medicine as a cure for the sick is equipment for maintaining life
vsm1.1:96.12:
because it protects by preventing the arising of affliction destructive to life; and it
is an accessory too because it is an instrument for prolonging life.
vsm1.1:96.13: That is why it is called “requisite.”
vsm1.1:96.14: So it is medicine as cure for the sick and that is a requisite, thus it is a “requisite of medicine as cure for the sick.”
vsm1.1:96.15: He makes use of that requisite of medicine as cure for the sick;
vsm1.1:96.16:
any requisite for life consisting of oil, honey, molasses, ghee, etc.,
that is allowed by a medical man as suitable for the sick, is what is meant.
vsm1.1:97.1: 97. From arisen: from born, become, produced.
vsm1.1:97.2: Hurtful: here “hurt (affliction)” is a disturbance of elements,
vsm1.1:97.3: and it is the leprosy, tumours, boils, etc., originated by that disturbance.
vsm1.1:97.4: Hurtful (veyyābādhika) because arisen in the form of hurt (byābādha).
vsm1.1:97.5: Feelings: painful feelings, feelings resulting from unprofitable kamma
vsm1.1:97.7: For complete immunity from affliction: for complete freedom from pain;
vsm1.1:97.8: so that all that is painful is abandoned, is the meaning.
vsm1.1:97.9:
This is how this virtue concerning requisites should be understood. In brief
its characteristic is the use of requisites after wise reflection.
vsm1.1:97.10:
The word-meaning here is this: because breathing things go (ayanti), move, proceed, using what they
use in dependence on these robes, etc., these robes, etc., are therefore called requisites (paccaya = ger. of paṭi + ayati);
